title: Pay real estate and personal property taxes
question: When are real estate and personal property (car) taxes due in Staunton, and how can I pay them?
summary: Staunton's elected City Treasurer bills and collects real estate and personal property taxes. The Commissioner of the Revenue values vehicles and other personal property, and the City Assessor values real estate. Real estate tax is due 75% on June 20 and 25% on December 5. Personal property (car) tax is due December 5. If the office is closed on a due date, pay the next business day. Pay online or by phone (provider fees: card 2.35%, e-check $0.25), by mail to P.O. Box 474, in the green drop box on Central Avenue, or at the Treasurer's Office in City Hall. For help call 540.332.3833. Late payments add penalty and interest. Value disputes go to the Commissioner or Assessor.

steps.step: Note the real estate due dates: 75% on June 20 and 25% on December 5
steps.who: Property owner; City Treasurer (bills and collects)
steps.how: Real estate tax is billed on the value assessed as of January 1. Bills usually go out in early May. Three quarters of the year's tax is due June 20 and the last quarter December 5. The tax is the assessed value divided by 100, times the rate set by City Council (currently $0.91). Example from the city: a property assessed at $251,240 owes $2,286.28 a year.
steps.quote: Seventy-five percent of the tax bill is due on June 20th, with the remaining 25% due on the following December 5th.

steps.step: Note the personal property (car) tax due date: December 5, in one payment
steps.who: Vehicle owners and businesses; Commissioner of the Revenue (values the property); City Treasurer (bills and collects)
steps.how: Personal property is taxed as of January 1 (the tax day in state law). The Commissioner values vehicles from the January J.D. Power guide, using clean trade value when it is available and otherwise a percentage of cost. The rate is $2.90 per $100 of assessed value. Qualifying vehicles get state car tax relief (PPTRA) on the first $20,000 of value, at a reduced rate the city sets. Under state law a qualifying vehicle is a passenger car, motorcycle, autocycle, or pickup or panel truck that the Commissioner finds is owned or leased by an individual for non-business use (or held in a private trust for non-business purposes). The bill must say whether the vehicle qualifies. Business personal property is also paid by December 5; the business return is due May 1 (a separate process).
steps.fee: $2.90 per $100 of assessed value, less car tax relief on qualifying vehicles
steps.quote: Tax bills are due by December 5 of the current year.

steps.step: If a due date falls on a day the office is closed, pay by the next business day
steps.how: The city accepts payment without penalty on the next business day when a due date falls on a day the Treasurer's Office is closed. State law has the same rule for weekends, legal holidays and office closures.
steps.deadline: The next business day after a due date that falls on a closed day
steps.quote: If a due date falls on a day that the office is closed payments are accepted next business day without penalty.

steps.step: Receive the bill by mail; if a mortgage company pays from escrow, it gets the bill
steps.who: City Treasurer; mortgage company (escrow); property owner
steps.how: State law requires the Treasurer to mail bills at least 14 days before the due date. For escrowed real estate, bills go to the mortgage company a little earlier and the whole escrow amount is due June 20. If the lender does not pay, state law says a past-due bill goes to the owner. The Treasurer may decide not to mail a bill of $20 or less. The pages and law read do not say that a missing bill moves a due date, so call the Treasurer if a bill has not arrived.
steps.deadline: Bill mailed no later than 14 days before the due date (state law)
steps.quote: Tax bills that are the responsibility of mortgage companies (who have loaned the money for the property) are sent a little earlier, and the entire escrow amount is due on June 20th.

steps.step: Check the bill, and take any dispute about the value to the office that assessed it
steps.who: Taxpayer; Commissioner of the Revenue (personal property values, car tax relief); City Assessor (real estate values)
steps.how: The Treasurer collects what has been assessed but does not set values. Questions about a vehicle, its value or car tax relief go to the Commissioner of the Revenue (540.332.3829). Questions about a real estate value go to the City Assessor (540.332.3827), with appeal deadlines printed on the notice of assessment. Under state law, while an application to the Commissioner for correction (Va. Code § 58.1-3980) filed within 90 days of the assessment is pending, and for 30 days after the decision, the bill is not treated as delinquent or sent to collection; interest may still be charged afterwards on any part found to be owed. See the escalation rungs.
steps.deadline: Correction: within three years from the end of the tax year or one year from the assessment, whichever is later (state law); real estate appeals by the dates on the notice of assessment
steps.quote: The Commissioner of Revenue calculates the value of personal property, business personal property and machinery and tools and processes state income tax returns.

steps.who: Taxpayer; the city's third-party payment provider
steps.how: Open the city's Tyler self-service site for real estate. Search for the bill by address, owner name or parcel ID; the site advises searching by parcel ID alone if results are not as expected. Pay by credit or debit card or by e-check. The provider charges the fee. Keep the confirmation number: the site says that a confirmation number means the payment went through.
steps.deadline: By the due date (June 20 and December 5)
steps.fee: 2.35% for credit or debit card; $0.25 per e-check transaction (charged by the service provider)
steps.quote: Real Estate bills may be searched by Address (all or partial), Name (all or partial), and/or Parcel ID.

steps.step: Pay personal property tax online (needs a web user account)
steps.who: Taxpayer; the city's third-party payment provider
steps.how: Online payment of personal property tax needs a web user account on the city's self-service site. Create the account, then link your personal property account(s) to it. The city posts two instruction documents, one for a new account and one for re-linking an account. If linked accounts do not show, the city says to log off and log back on. The same provider fees apply.
steps.fee: 2.35% for credit or debit card; $0.25 per e-check transaction (charged by the service provider)
steps.quote: Online payment of personal property taxes requires a web user account.

steps.step: Or pay by phone, any time
steps.who: Taxpayer; the city's third-party payment provider
steps.how: Call 1.888.272.9829 (24 hours a day). Select option 3, enter jurisdiction code 1038, then press 1 for personal property or 2 for real estate. Enter the invoice number followed by #, the amount followed by #, and the card number and expiration date. Discover, VISA, MasterCard, American Express and e-check are accepted. Save the verbal receipt number the system gives you.
steps.fee: 2.35% for credit or debit card; $0.25 per e-check transaction (charged by the service provider)
steps.quote: Real estate and personal property taxes and utility bills can be paid via phone with your credit card by calling 1.888.272.9829.

steps.how: Mail a check or money order payable to the City of Staunton to the Treasurer at P.O. Box 474, Staunton, VA 24402-0474. Under state law a payment mailed in a sealed envelope that is postmarked (or has a commercial delivery service's confirmation of shipment) by midnight of the due date is on time. If, through no fault of yours, the envelope has no postmark or an illegible or undated one, it is on time if it arrives by mail within five days after the close of business on the due date. A USPS Certificate of Mailing or other proof of mailing also shows the payment was on time.
steps.deadline: Postmarked by the due date (state law)
steps.quote: Check or money order made payable to the City of Staunton can be mailed to:

steps.step: Or use a city drop box
steps.how: Put a check or money order (no cash) in the green drop box on Central Avenue under the clock tower, which is open 24 hours a day. During business hours there is also a drop box inside City Hall in front of the Treasurer's Office. The drop box at Public Works on Craigmont Road takes utility payments only.
steps.quote: Drop your check or money order in the City’s green drop box located on Central Avenue under the clock tower or inside of City Hall in front of the Treasurer’s office during business hours.

steps.step: Or pay in person at City Hall
steps.how: Go to the Treasurer's Office on the first floor of City Hall (Beverley Street entrance), 116 W. Beverley Street, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday to Friday. If you plan to pay with a large number of coins, read the city's coin acceptance policy first. State law entitles you to a receipt on request.
steps.deadline: By the due date, during office hours
steps.quote: Visit the Treasurer’s Office on the first floor of City Hall, 116 W. Beverley Street, between 8:30 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday.

steps.step: If you need help paying, call the Treasurer's Office before the due date
steps.how: Call 540.332.3833, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday to Friday. The city's pages do not describe a payment plan. Owners aged 65 or older, or permanently and totally disabled, may qualify for real estate tax relief from the Commissioner of the Revenue; the application deadline is May 1 (a separate process).
steps.quote: If you need assistance with paying your personal property or real estate taxes, please call 540.332.3833 between 8:30 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday.

steps.step: If you pay late: a penalty and interest are added
steps.how: The city's pages that were read do not give Staunton's penalty or interest rates. City Code § 3.10.040 covers them but was not read (see caveats). State law sets the caps: a penalty of up to 10% of the tax past due, or up to 25% on personal property more than 30 days past due, or $10 if that is more, but never more than the tax. Interest is capped at 10% a year in the first year, starting no earlier than the day after the due date. The penalty may be added the day after the first installment is due and becomes part of the tax. Unless a city ordinance says otherwise, state law credits a payment first to the oldest delinquent account that is still collectible.
steps.deadline: Penalty may be assessed the day after the due date (state law)
steps.fee: Staunton's rates not published on the pages read; state caps: penalty 10% (25% for personal property more than 30 days late) or $10, interest 10% a year in the first year
steps.quote: No penalty for failure to pay a tax or installment shall exceed (1) 10 percent of the tax past due on such property

steps.step: Ask the Treasurer to remove a penalty that was not your fault
steps.how: State law bars penalty and interest when the late payment was not the taxpayer's fault, and the Treasurer decides fault for late payment. Death or a medically determinable physical or mental impairment on the due date is presumed to be no fault if the tax is paid within 30 days of the due date; if a guardian, conservator or other fiduciary handles the person's affairs, the tax must be paid within 120 days after the fiduciary qualifies or begins to act. Interest still runs until the tax is paid in full. No penalty or interest applies if you show a USPS Certificate of Mailing or other proof of mailing by the due date. No penalty applies to an assessment made less than two weeks before the due date through a local official's fault, if it is paid within two weeks after notice. The city publishes no waiver form or policy, so call the Treasurer's Office or write to P.O. Box 474 with your reasons and supporting documents.
steps.deadline: None stated; for the death or impairment presumption, pay within 30 days of the due date (120 days after a fiduciary qualifies)
steps.quote: The treasurer shall make determinations of fault relating exclusively to failure to pay a tax

steps.step: If you are deployed outside the United States with the armed forces: automatic extension
steps.how: State law requires an automatic extension for members of the U.S. armed services deployed outside the United States. It covers real estate tax on a primary residence and personal property tax on a qualifying vehicle. Active duty in the regular forces, the National Guard and the reserves all count. The taxes become due 90 days after the deployment ends. The city's pages do not say how to tell the Treasurer, so call the office.
steps.quote: Such extension shall end and the taxes shall be due 90 days following the completion of such member's deployment.

steps.step: If taxes stay unpaid: collection, and in the end a court sale of the real estate
steps.who: City Treasurer (collection); Staunton Circuit Court (tax sale)
steps.how: State law lets the Treasurer collect unpaid taxes by distress. Once taxes are more than 30 days delinquent, the Treasurer can send a treasurer's lien to an employer, bank or anyone else holding the taxpayer's money; a lien on wages is generally limited to 25% of disposable earnings per pay period. If the city has an agreement with DMV, unpaid personal property tax can block vehicle registration, after a notice at least 30 days before the registration expires. Administrative costs may be added (City Code § 3.05.090; state cap $30 before judgment, $35 after), and attorney's or collection agency fees of up to 20% of the amount collected. Real estate delinquent on December 31 after the second anniversary of the due date may be sold by court order (after the first anniversary for condemned, nuisance, derelict or blighted property). At least 30 days before going to court, the Treasurer must send a notice saying the owner may ask the Treasurer for a payment agreement of up to 72 months; the Treasurer may suspend the sale action under such an agreement. The owner can redeem before the sale date by paying all taxes, penalties, interest and costs; a partial payment does not redeem. The city's pages do not describe its own collection practice.
steps.deadline: Treasurer's lien after 30 days delinquent; tax sale after December 31 following the second anniversary of the due date; collection limit 5 years (20 years for real estate)
steps.fee: Administrative costs up to $30 before judgment and $35 after (state cap); Staunton's amounts not read
steps.quote: When any taxes on any real estate in a locality are delinquent on December 31 following the second anniversary of the date on which such taxes have become due

escalation.next: City Treasurer: ask for a payment agreement of up to 72 months. The Treasurer may agree, and may then suspend the sale action; the case stays on the court's docket until the agreement is paid, and a default lets the Treasurer void it on 15 days' written notice.
escalation.deadline: The notice comes at least 30 days before the Treasurer starts court proceedings; redemption is possible until the sale date
escalation.quote: Such notice shall advise the taxpayer that the taxpayer may request the treasurer to enter into a payment agreement to permit the payment of the delinquent taxes, interest, and penalties over a period not to exceed 72 months in accordance with the provisions of subsection C.

escalation.trigger: You cannot pay in full, and collecting the entire amount is in substantial doubt (the Treasurer must also find that a compromise serves the city's best interests)
escalation.next: City Treasurer: a written offer in compromise, which needs the consent of City Council or its designee and is accepted only by written notice. The city's pages read do not mention offers in compromise.
escalation.quote: Any offer in compromise submitted to an official responsible for the assessment or collection of local taxes shall be made in writing and shall be deemed accepted only when the taxpayer is notified in writing of the acceptance by the responsible official.

escalation.trigger: The personal property (vehicle) amount is wrong: wrong value, vehicle sold or moved, or wrong car tax relief status
escalation.next: Commissioner of the Revenue (application for correction). While an application filed within 90 days of the assessment is pending, and for 30 days after the decision, the bill is not treated as delinquent or sent to collection; interest may still be charged on any part found to be owed.
escalation.deadline: Within three years from the last day of the tax year, or within one year from the date of the assessment, whichever is later
escalation.quote: apply to the commissioner of the revenue or such other official who made the assessment for a correction thereof.

escalation.trigger: An unpaid personal property bill is for a year in which you were not subject to the tax (for example, you had moved away)
escalation.next: Commissioner of the Revenue, which, if satisfied the assessment is wrong, abates it and notifies the Treasurer to correct the account or refund
escalation.deadline: At any time while the tax is still collectible (five years after December 31 of the tax year)
escalation.quote: an unpaid tangible personal property tax assessment may be appealed to the commissioner of the revenue or other assessing official at any time during which such assessment is collectible under § 58.1-3940 , provided the taxpayer can demonstrate by clear factual evidence that he was not subject to the tax for the year in question.

escalation.trigger: You disagree with the real estate assessment behind the bill
escalation.next: City Assessor's Office: review of the assessment (call, visit or email the appeals mailbox)
escalation.deadline: By the date on the notice of assessment; for the 2026 notices, 5 p.m. on March 23, 2026
escalation.quote: Requests for review of the revised assessment must be made to the City Assessor by March 23, 2026.

escalation.trigger: You still disagree after the Assessor's review
escalation.next: Board of Equalization (appeal forms only from the Assessor's Office; Va. Code § 58.1-3378)
escalation.deadline: By the date on the notice of assessment; for 2026, 5 p.m. on April 23, 2026
escalation.quote: Appeals to the Board of Equalization must be filed by April 23, 2026.

escalation.trigger: You are still aggrieved by an assessment (for real estate, the city's FAQ describes the Circuit Court as the next step after the Board of Equalization)
escalation.next: Staunton Circuit Court (application for relief from an erroneous assessment, filed with the Clerk of the Circuit Court)
escalation.deadline: Whichever is latest of: three years from the last day of the tax year; one year from the date of the assessment; one year from a final determination by the Commissioner under § 58.1-3981
escalation.quote: apply for relief to the circuit court of the county or city wherein such assessment was made.

caveats: The City of Staunton's website (www.ci.staunton.va.us) refuses automated readers, so the city pages and PDFs cited here are Internet Archive copies: they show the pages as they were when copied. The city-page quotes are matched to the newest copy of each cited page (from April 13 to September 16, 2026; listed in sources). The Tyler real estate payment page is read live. Anything on this page that those copies do not hold is marked as not confirmed. The live pages may have changed since; confirm on them or by phone before you act.

Local ordinance not quoted. Staunton's City Code is on General Code's eCode360. Its terms limit content to personal use and forbid reproducing it for public purposes. Only the table of contents of Title 3 has been checked, for section numbers and links (§§ 3.10.040, 3.10.015, 3.05.090, 3.05.070, 3.55.010). No section text is quoted, and the descriptions are lexflow's paraphrases of the headings. Staunton's penalty rate, interest rate, collection fees and returned-check fee are therefore not stated here; the state caps are given instead.

Unequal installments. The city's pages say 75% of the real estate tax is due June 20 and 25% on December 5. Va. Code § 58.1-3916 speaks of 'a single installment or in two equal installments' and is the 'sole authority' for local due dates. City Code § 3.10.040 has not been checked, and the authority for the 75/25 split is not settled here. The dates here are the city's.

Default penalty if no ordinance applied. Without a local ordinance, state law sets a 5% penalty (Va. Code § 58.1-3915) and 10% a year interest (§ 58.1-3918). City Code § 3.10.040's heading refers to penalty and interest on delinquent taxes, so the city's own rates probably apply; they were not confirmed.

Rates and year. The Taxes page and the Real Estate Tax FAQs give $0.91 per $100 for real estate, the FAQ calling it 'currently' the rate. The Historical Tax Rates table ends with 2025 ($0.91). The Assessor's appeal page announced an April 9, 2026 public hearing before any change in the rate, and the 2026 rate was not confirmed. The $2.90 personal property rate carries no year. The Personal Property page gives the car tax relief percentage only for 2023 (33%) and still describes the 2006 change to a fixed reimbursement. The Assessor's main page, in an Internet Archive copy of September 16, 2026 (after the hearing), still says 'The current real estate tax rate is $0.91 per hundred of assessed value.'

Not found on the pages read: whether Staunton charges a local vehicle license fee (City Code § 3.10.050 concerns vehicles without current license plates and was not read); whether the city prorates vehicle tax for vehicles that arrive or leave during the year (a local option under Va. Code § 58.1-3516); whether paperless or emailed bills are offered; which payment types (cash, card) are taken at the counter; whether the city uses DMV registration holds, treasurer's liens or a collection agency; and any payment plan or penalty waiver policy.

Online payment wording varies. The Taxes page says 'Pay by credit or debit card' online; the Paying Taxes & Fees page and the real estate payment site also accept e-check, at $0.25 per transaction. The phone line page says it accepts e-check too. Check the fee shown on the payment screen before paying.
Not confirmed: the two personal property account instruction PDFs and the coin acceptance policy PDF. Their titles and URLs come from the pages that link them; their contents are not described here.

Privacy. The city's mailing-address blocks name the Treasurer, and the office pages list the Treasurer's, the Commissioner's and the Assessor's personal mailboxes. Those names and mailboxes are omitted. No general Treasurer email address was found. The only email recorded is the Assessor's appeals mailbox, which the appeal page publishes as the office channel.

The Assessor's page gives P.O. Box 58 as its mailing address, the same box the Treasurer's page gives for utility payments (Utilities Dept). It is recorded as published; confirm before mailing anything to the Assessor.
Downtown Service District. The Assessor publishes a separate land book for the Downtown Service District additional tax (City Code § 3.60.020, not read). Its rate and how it is billed were not found.

Timeliness. The city's pages do not say how they treat postmarks or card payments that settle after the due date. Va. Code § 58.1-9(A) treats a payment postmarked (or shipped by a commercial delivery service) by midnight on the due date as on time, and § 58.1-9(B) treats an electronic funds transfer received by midnight on the due date as on time.

Escalation. No outside review of a Treasurer's refusal to waive a penalty was found. Va. Code § 58.1-3916 makes an assessed penalty part of the tax, but the sources read do not settle whether a refused waiver can go to the circuit court under § 58.1-3984. The Tax Commissioner appeal in § 58.1-3983.1 covers business and mobile property taxes, not individual car tax. The assessment-appeal deadlines given are those for the 394 parcels that got 2026 change notices; the next general reassessment is effective January 1, 2027.

Circuit Court. The city's Real Estate Tax FAQs say an owner not satisfied with the Board of Equalization 'may appeal further to the local Circuit Court', filed with the Clerk of the Circuit Court. Va. Code § 58.1-3984(A) sets its own deadlines (three years from the end of the tax year, one year from the assessment, or one year from a final determination under § 58.1-3981). The sources read do not say whether the local steps must be used before going to court.

Business personal property and machinery and tools are paid by December 5 like other personal property, but the May 1 return to the Commissioner is a separate process. Real estate tax relief for elderly and disabled owners (application by May 1) and the rehabilitation abatement are also separate processes.

Staunton is an independent city surrounded by Augusta County. Some properties with a Staunton mailing address may lie in Augusta County and be taxed by the county, not the city. Check that the property is inside city limits.
State law. Code of Virginia quotes are from Open US Law's copy of the cited section. The law.lis.virginia.gov URLs are given for reference.
All city pages were read on 2026-10-11. Due dates, rates and fees change with City Council action; check the Treasurer's pages before relying on them.

corrections: Quotes: all 90 original quotes confirmed. The 70 state-law quotes (54 legal_basis, 4 steps, 6 fees, 6 escalation rungs) are whitespace-normalised substrings of I.text_of for the cited section, and the subsection labels match the text. lexflow's own checker (municipal.places.check_quotes) also matched 83 of 83 code quotes after the edits. The 20 city-page quotes were matched character for character (curly apostrophes included) against the latest Internet Archive copies of the cited pages, fetched 2026-10-11 with the research User-Agent, and the s6 quote against the live Tyler real estate page. The 13 quotes added below were checked the same way against I.text_of.

Live checks of claims without quotes: the J.D. Power method, the phone keypad sequence, card brands, the drop box hours and the Craigmont Road utility-only box, the Treasurer's Beverley Street entrance, the fax and phone numbers, the P.O. boxes, the $251,240 example, early-May billing, the 394 change notices and 5 p.m. appeal times, and the tax relief May 1 deadline (Tax Relief FAQs, archive copy 2026-07-17) all match the archived pages. The five City Code section numbers and headings match the eCode360 Title 3 table of contents (headings only; no section text read).

s2: the qualifying-vehicle description ('privately owned or leased passenger cars, motorcycles and pickups') was narrower than Va. Code § 58.1-3523. It now follows the definition: a passenger car, motorcycle, autocycle, or pickup or panel truck owned or leased by an individual for non-business use, or held in a private trust for non-business purposes. 'At a percentage the city sets' is now 'at a reduced rate the city sets' (§ 58.1-3524(C)(2)).

s4: removed two claims no source supports: that a $20-or-less bill 'is still owed' and that 'not getting a bill does not change the due date'. Neither the city pages nor the Code sections read say so (an index search found no failure-to-receive rule). The step now says the sources do not say a missing bill moves a due date and advises calling the Treasurer.

s5 and escalation rung 4: 'stops collection until 30 days after the decision' overstated § 58.1-3958 / § 58.1-3916. Those sections say the bill is not deemed delinquent or subject to collection while a § 58.1-3980 appeal filed within 90 days is pending and for 30 days after, and they keep interest on any amount found owed. s5 also now says the rule covers an application to the Commissioner, not the Assessor review. A legal_basis entry was added for the interest proviso.
s9: added the state-law five-day rule for a missing, illegible or undated postmark (§ 58.1-9(A)) and proof by a USPS Certificate of Mailing (§ 58.1-3916), with legal_basis entries.
s13: added the § 58.1-3913 rule that a payment is credited first to the oldest delinquent collectible account unless an ordinance says otherwise (already in legal_basis but not in any step).

s14 and escalation rung 1: added the 120-day rule when a fiduciary handles the taxpayer's affairs, that interest still accrues, and the proof-of-mailing bar (§ 58.1-3916). The 30-day death or impairment rule is now described as a condition of the presumption of no fault, not as a deadline that must be met in every case. Legal_basis entries added.

s16: 'a notice offering a payment agreement' overstated § 58.1-3965(A). The notice tells the owner they may ask the Treasurer for one, and the Treasurer may suspend the sale action under an agreement (§ 58.1-3965(C)). Added the first-anniversary sale route for condemned, nuisance, derelict or blighted property (§ 58.1-3965(A)), the rule that a partial payment does not redeem (§ 58.1-3965(B)), the general 25% limit on wage liens (§ 58.1-3952(B)), the DMV notice at least 30 days before the registration expires (§ 46.2-752(J)), and the 20% cap on attorney's or collection agency fees (§ 58.1-3958). Legal_basis entries added.

Escalation rung 2: the payment agreement is at the Treasurer's discretion ('may'); added that the case stays on the court's docket during the agreement (§ 58.1-3965(D)) and that a default lets the Treasurer void it on 15 days' written notice (§ 58.1-3965(E)).

Escalation rung 3 (offer in compromise): removed the invented example '(for example, serious hardship)'. The trigger now follows § 58.1-3994(B): collection of the entire amount in substantial doubt, and a compromise in the city's best interests. Added the written-acceptance rule (§ 58.1-3994(C)), and that the city pages read do not mention offers in compromise.

Escalation rung 8 (Circuit Court): removed '(the court does not require them first)', which neither § 58.1-3984 nor a city page says. The city FAQ describes the court as the step after the Board of Equalization; a caveat now says the sources do not settle whether the local steps are required first. The deadline said 'one year from ... the final local determination'. § 58.1-3984(A)(d) runs from a final determination under § 58.1-3981 (the Commissioner's correction), so the deadline is restated, with a legal_basis entry.

Fees: added the state cap on attorney's or collection agency fees (20% of the amount collected, § 58.1-3958). The additional-receipt fee now notes the § 58.1-3914 exception for the year the real estate is transferred.

Caveats and sources: the access caveat records how verification was done; the rates caveat adds that the Assessor's page (archive copy 2026-09-16, after the April 9 hearing) still calls $0.91 the current rate; a Circuit Court caveat was added. The 11 Internet Archive copies used were added to sources.

Privacy: no staff names, personal mailboxes or direct lines. The Treasurer's name in the city's mailing-address blocks and the officials' names on the office pages are left out. The only email is the Assessor's function mailbox assessmentappeal@, which the appeal page publishes for appeals. Schema: valid JSON in the same shape as the verified Charlottesville and Albemarle files; step ids s1 to s16 unique; forms f1 and f3 referenced by steps exist (f2 is listed for s7's second instruction document).
open_issues: www.ci.staunton.va.us still refuses the research User-Agent (HTTP 403, robots.txt included). The verifier checked every city page against Internet Archive copies dated 2026-04-13 to 2026-09-16, not the live site, so changes after those dates would be missed. The modeller's reading of the live site through the desktop browser pane is for the user to accept or not.

Staunton City Code (eCode360) not read under its terms: Staunton's penalty and interest rates (§ 3.10.040), collection and returned-check fees (§§ 3.05.090, 3.05.070) and the car tax relief ordinance (§ 3.10.015) are not stated; the state caps are given instead.

The city's 75% / 25% real estate installments sit uneasily with the 'two equal installments' wording of Va. Code § 58.1-3916; the local authority was not worked out. This does not change the dates the city publishes and enforces.

Not published on the pages read: the 2026 car tax relief percentage (only 2023's 33% is given), the year of the $2.90 rate, a penalty waiver form or policy, a payment plan for current taxes, the city's collection practice (DMV holds, liens, collection agency), and the Downtown Service District rate.
The two personal property account instruction PDFs (f1, f2) and the coin acceptance policy PDF (f3) were not opened; their titles and URLs come from the linking pages.
